🚗 Health Insurance Cross-Sell Prediction — Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Dataset: Health Insurance Cross Sell Prediction (Kaggle — Anmol Kumar) Target: Response — Will the health-insurance customer buy vehicle insurance? Author: Narendra Kalam

🏦 Business Problem¶

An insurance company that already provides Health Insurance to ~381,000 customers wants to know which of them would also be interested in Vehicle Insurance. Cross-selling to an existing, already-trusting customer base is far cheaper than cold-acquisition — but blind outreach (calling every customer) wastes agent time and irritates people who will never convert.

Companies like Bajaj Allianz, HDFC Ergo and Policybazaar run this exact workflow: score the existing book, rank by propensity, and route only the high-probability names to telecallers.

Key challenges:

  • Only 12.3% of existing customers respond positively — a call center dialing at random converts roughly 1 in 8 calls
  • The dataset mixes binary flags (Driving_License, Previously_Insured, Vehicle_Damage), high-cardinality categoricals (Region_Code — 53 levels, Policy_Sales_Channel — 155 levels) and skewed continuous fields (Annual_Premium)
  • Previously_Insured and Vehicle_Damage interact almost deterministically — a customer who is already insured and has no damage history essentially never converts
  • The channel that reaches a customer (agent call, mailer, in-person) matters more than raw demographics for some segments

Goal: Build a classifier that ranks customers by cross-sell propensity, so telecalling effort concentrates on the top-decile leads — reducing cold-calling cost by 60–70% while lifting the conversion rate several times over the 12.3% baseline.

Step 1 — Import Libraries¶

Why: All required libraries imported upfront. scipy.stats enables statistical hypothesis testing beyond basic descriptive statistics; statsmodels powers the VIF multicollinearity check.

In [1]:

Step 2 — Data Loading and Initial Inspection¶

Why: First look at raw data — shape, column names, and transposed head() for easy reading when many columns exist.

Business context: The dataset contains 381,109 existing health-insurance customers. Each row is one customer, with demographic fields (age, gender), policy history (vintage, previously insured), vehicle risk signals (vehicle age, past damage), and the outreach channel used.

Step 3 — Dataset Structure and Data Types¶

Why: Understanding dtypes is critical before any transformation. Binary columns (0/1) must be identified early so SMOTENC treats them correctly — not interpolating between 0 and 1. High-cardinality categoricals (region_code, policy_sales_channel) need a different encoding strategy than low-cardinality ones.

In [3]:

    'null_count': df_raw.isna().sum(), 'unique_vals': df_raw.nunique(),
    'sample_vals': df_raw.apply(lambda c: c.dropna().unique()[:3].tolist())
})

📌 Observation: gender, vehicle_age, vehicle_damage are the only object columns (2, 3, and 2 categories respectively). region_code has 53 unique values and policy_sales_channel has 155 — far too many for one-hot encoding without exploding dimensionality. driving_license and previously_insured are already binary integers.

💡 Pipeline decision: gender→binary map, vehicle_damage→binary map, vehicle_age→ordinal map (< 1 Year < 1-2 Year < > 2 Years). region_code and policy_sales_channel → target/frequency encoding, never one-hot — 53+155 dummy columns would dominate the feature space.

Step 4 — Missing Values Analysis¶

Why: Missing values must be identified before modeling. Visualizing with a heatmap is faster than reading numeric counts — patterns across rows reveal systematic missingness.

Business insight: A missing annual_premium or region_code in a live feed usually means an upstream data-entry gap at the branch, not a genuine "no premium" customer — worth flagging for the ops team rather than silently imputing.

In [4]:
missing_counts = df_raw.isnull().sum()
missing_pct    = df_raw.isnull().mean() * 100

📌 Observation: Zero missing values across all 12 columns — a clean, well-curated insurance-book export.

💡 Pipeline decision: No imputation needed for training. validate_input_data() still checks for nulls in every incoming column to handle future data drift, since live branch feeds are not guaranteed to stay this clean.

Step 5 — Duplicate Detection and Data Cleaning¶

Why: Duplicate rows can artificially inflate model performance during cross-validation — the same customer profile appearing in both train and validation sets is a subtle form of data leakage. id is checked separately since it is unique by construction and would mask duplicate detection if left in.

In [5]:
dupes_incl_id = df_raw.duplicated().sum()
dupes_excl_id = df_raw.drop(columns=['id']).duplicated().sum()
print(f'Duplicate rows (including id)    : {dupes_incl_id}')
print(f'Duplicate rows (excluding id)    : {dupes_excl_id}')

df = df_raw.copy()
df.drop(columns=['id'], inplace=True)

print(f'\nShape before cleaning : {df_raw.shape}')
print(f'Shape after  cleaning : {df.shape}')
print(f'Response rate         : {df["response"].mean():.4f} ({df["response"].mean()*100:.2f}%)')

Duplicate rows (including id)    : 0
Duplicate rows (excluding id)    : 269

Shape before cleaning : (381109, 12)
Shape after  cleaning : (381109, 11)
Response rate         : 0.1226 (12.26%)

📌 Observation: Zero duplicates on the full row (id is unique per record, as expected). 269 rows share an identical feature profile once id is excluded — with only 12 columns over 381K customers, some customers genuinely have the same age/premium/region/channel combination by chance. These are not data-entry errors and are kept.

💡 Pipeline decision: id dropped as a non-predictive identifier before any modeling. Rows are not dropped on feature-only duplication — two real customers can legitimately share a profile, and removing them would bias the response rate.

Step 6 — Statistical Summary Heatmap¶

Why: Descriptive statistics across features with very different scales are hard to compare in table form. A normalized heatmap makes it immediately visible which features have the widest spread or most extreme values.

Business insight: annual_premium has by far the widest range and highest coefficient of variation — premium amount varies enormously across the customer base and is a natural candidate for outlier handling and transformation.

In [6]:
num_cols_desc = ['age', 'annual_premium', 'vintage', 'region_code', 'policy_sales_channel']
desc = df[num_cols_desc].describe().T
desc['cv']    = (desc['std'] / desc['mean'].abs()).round(3)
desc['range'] = (desc['max'] - desc['min']).round(2)
print('Statistical Summary:'); display(desc.round(3))

cols_to_plot = ['mean', 'std', 'min', '25%', '50%', '75%', 'max']
heat_data = desc[cols_to_plot].apply(lambda x: (x - x.min()) / (x.max() - x.min() + 1e-9))

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
sns.heatmap(heat_data, annot=desc[cols_to_plot].round(1),
            fmt='g', cmap='YlOrRd', linewidths=0.5, linecolor='white')
plt.title('Step 6 — Statistical Summary Heatmap (Normalized)\n'
          'Darker = higher relative value. High range + high std → outlier clipping needed.',
          fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

annual_premium 381109.0 30564.390 17213.155 2630.0 24405.0 31669.0 39400.0 540165.0 0.563 537535.0

📌 Observation: The normalized heatmap and CV column confirm annual_premium has the widest absolute range (min 2,630 → max 540,165, a spread of ≈537.5K) and the highest coefficient of variation (CV = 0.563), followed closely by vintage (CV = 0.542), region_code (CV = 0.501), and policy_sales_channel (CV = 0.484). age has the lowest relative spread (CV = 0.400). policy_sales_channel and region_code are numeric-looking but are really categorical codes — their mean/std are not meaningful and must not be scaled as continuous features.

💡 Pipeline decision: annual_premium → IQR-based Clipper before scaling, driven by its extreme range. region_code/policy_sales_channel are excluded from the "continuous" preprocessing branch entirely and routed to categorical encoding instead, despite their numeric dtype.

Step 7 — Class Imbalance Analysis¶

Why: This is the most critical insight for model design. A model predicting "No" for every customer achieves 87.7% accuracy with 0% recall on the customers who would actually convert — completely useless for a telecalling campaign that needs a ranked lead list.

Business insight: A 12.3% base response rate is actually a good starting point for cross-sell (cold outreach campaigns often convert below 5%) — the model's job is to concentrate that 12.3% into the top of a ranked list, not to fix an extreme rarity problem.

In [7]:
counts = df['response'].value_counts().sort_index()
pct    = df['response'].value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index() * 100

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 5))

for bar, v, p in zip(bars, counts.values, pct.values):
    axes[0].text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width()/2, bar.get_height() + 3000,
                 f'{v:,}\n({p:.1f}%)', ha='center', fontweight='bold', fontsize=12)
axes[0].set_title('Class Count'); axes[0].set_ylabel('Count')
axes[0].set_ylim(0, counts.max() * 1.2)

axes[1].pie(counts.values, labels=['Not Interested (87.7%)', 'Interested (12.3%)'],
            colors=[BLUE, PINK], startangle=90,
            wedgeprops={'edgecolor': 'white', 'linewidth': 2},
            autopct='%1.1f%%', textprops={'fontsize': 11})
axes[1].set_title('Class Proportion')

ratio     = counts[0] / counts[1]
dummy_acc = counts[0] / counts.sum() * 100
scenarios = ['Dummy model\n(predict all 0)', 'Ranked model\n(SMOTENC + PR-AUC)']

axes[2].bar(np.arange(2) + 0.15, [0, 78.0], 0.3, label='Recall % (interested=1)', color=PINK, alpha=0.8)
axes[2].set_xticks(np.arange(2)); axes[2].set_xticklabels(scenarios, fontsize=10)
axes[2].set_title('Why Accuracy is Misleading\nRecall=0% despite 87.7% accuracy')
axes[2].set_ylabel('%'); axes[2].legend(fontsize=9); axes[2].set_ylim(0, 115)

plt.suptitle(f'Step 7 — Class Imbalance Analysis\nImbalance ratio {ratio:.1f}:1 → F1 + PR-AUC used. SMOTENC on training set only.',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f'Imbalance ratio : {ratio:.1f}:1')
print(f'Dummy accuracy  : {dummy_acc:.1f}% with 0% recall on interested customers')

Imbalance ratio : 7.2:1
Dummy accuracy  : 87.7% with 0% recall on interested customers

📌 Observation: 7.2:1 imbalance — 87.7% not interested vs 12.3% interested. The third panel shows why accuracy is deceptive: a dummy "always No" model already scores 87.7% accuracy while catching zero real leads.

💡 Pipeline decision: SMOTENC on the training fold only. PR-AUC and F1 (not accuracy) as primary selection metrics, since the business use case is ranking leads by propensity, not maximizing raw accuracy.

Step 8 — Continuous Feature Distributions (Univariate)¶

Why: Distribution shape determines the right preprocessing. Normal → StandardScaler. Right-skewed → PowerTransformer first. This step directly motivates the dual preprocessor architecture.

Business insight: annual_premium being right-skewed mirrors real insurance-book economics — most customers cluster around standard premium tiers, while a small number of high-value policies pull the tail far to the right.

In [8]:
cont_cols = ['age', 'annual_premium', 'vintage']
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(17, 9))

for i, col in enumerate(cont_cols):
    skew = df[col].skew(); kurt = df[col].kurtosis()
    color = PINK if abs(skew) > 1 else BLUE
    sns.histplot(df[col], kde=True, bins=40, color=color, edgecolor='white', ax=axes[0, i])
    axes[0, i].set_title(f'{col}\nskewness={skew:.2f}  kurtosis={kurt:.2f}', fontweight='bold')
    skew_label = 'RIGHT SKEWED ⚠' if skew > 1 else 'LEFT SKEWED ⚠' if skew < -1 else 'APPROX NORMAL ✅'
    axes[0, i].text(0.97, 0.95, skew_label, transform=axes[0, i].transAxes,
                    ha='right', va='top', fontsize=8,
                    color=PINK if '⚠' in skew_label else GREEN, fontweight='bold')
    axes[1, i].boxplot(df[col].dropna(), patch_artist=True,
                       boxprops=dict(facecolor=color, alpha=0.6),
                       medianprops=dict(color='white', linewidth=2.5),
                       whiskerprops=dict(color=color), capprops=dict(color=color),
                       flierprops=dict(marker='o', markerfacecolor=GRAY, markersize=3, alpha=0.4))
    axes[1, i].set_title(f'{col} — boxplot')
    q1, q3 = df[col].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    n_out  = ((df[col] < q1-1.5*(q3-q1)) | (df[col] > q3+1.5*(q3-q1))).sum()
    axes[1, i].set_xlabel(f'{n_out} outliers detected')

plt.suptitle('Step 8 — Continuous Feature Distributions (Univariate)\n'
             'Pink = skewed (|skew|>1) → PowerTransformer applied. Blue = approx normal → StandardScaler only.',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

📌 Observation: annual_premium is strongly right-skewed (skew ≈ 1.77) with 10,320 IQR outliers (2.7% of the book). age is moderately right-skewed (skew ≈ 0.67, younger customer base). vintage is almost perfectly uniform (skew ≈ 0.00) — it looks like a designed/sampled field rather than an organic tenure distribution.

💡 Pipeline decision: annual_premium → PowerTransformer(yeo-johnson) in the scaled preprocessor for linear models. age and vintage need only clipping + scaling, no power transform. Tree models receive raw clipped values — scale/skew invariant.

Step 9 — Categorical/Binary Feature Analysis¶

Why: Binary and low-cardinality categorical features cannot be analyzed with histograms. The meaningful question is: "Does this attribute make the customer more or less likely to say yes?" Bars showing the response rate per group answer this directly.

Business insight: vehicle_damage and previously_insured turn out to be the two strongest business levers in the entire dataset — telecallers should sort call lists by these two flags first, before looking at anything else.

In [9]:
cat_cols     = ['gender', 'driving_license', 'previously_insured', 'vehicle_age', 'vehicle_damage']
overall_rate = df['response'].mean() * 100

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(18, 11))
axes = axes.flatten()

for i, col in enumerate(cat_cols):
    loan_rate    = df.groupby(col)['response'].mean() * 100
    count_by_grp = df[col].value_counts()
    order = loan_rate.index
    ax = axes[i]
    bars = ax.bar(order.astype(str), loan_rate.reindex(order).values,
                  color=[PINK if v > overall_rate else BLUE for v in loan_rate.reindex(order).values],
                  edgecolor='white', width=0.5)
    for bar, idx in zip(bars, order):
        cnt = count_by_grp[idx]
        ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width()/2, bar.get_height() + 0.6,
                f'{bar.get_height():.1f}%\n(n={cnt:,})',
                ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=9, fontweight='bold')
    ax.axhline(overall_rate, color='black', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5,
               label=f'Overall: {overall_rate:.1f}%')
    ax.set_title(f'{col}\nResponse Rate by Group', fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_ylabel('Response Rate (%)'); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
    ax.set_ylim(0, loan_rate.max() * 1.35)

axes[5].axis('off')
plt.suptitle('Step 9 — Categorical/Binary Feature Analysis\n'
             'Pink = above-average response rate. vehicle_damage and previously_insured dominate all other splits.',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

📌 Observation: Reading the exact bar values — vehicle_damage=Yes → 23.77% response vs vehicle_damage=No → 0.52% (a ~46× gap). previously_insured=0 → 22.55% vs previously_insured=1 → 0.09% (a ~250× gap, the single widest split in the whole dataset). vehicle_age rises monotonically with age of the vehicle: < 1 Year 4.37% → 1-2 Year 17.38% → > 2 Years 29.37%. driving_license=0 customers respond at only 5.05% vs 12.27% for licensed customers (overall rate 12.26%). gender shows the smallest gap of the five: Male 13.84% vs Female 10.39%.

💡 Pipeline decision: previously_insured and vehicle_damage are flagged as the two highest-priority features for the model and for a simple business rule: never call a customer with previously_insured=1 and vehicle_damage=No — that segment converts at under 0.1%. vehicle_age is kept as an ordinal feature (not one-hot) since its response rate increases monotonically with category order.

Step 10 — Bivariate Analysis: Continuous Features vs Target¶

Why: Overlapping KDE plots directly answer: "Where in the value range are interested customers concentrated?" Non-overlapping = strong predictor. Overlapping = weak discriminating power.

Business insight: Older customers convert somewhat better than younger ones — plausible, since older drivers are more likely to already own a vehicle worth insuring and to have experienced a claim.

In [10]:
cont_cols = ['age', 'annual_premium', 'vintage']
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 5))

for i, col in enumerate(cont_cols):
    no_resp = df[df['response']==0][col]
    resp    = df[df['response']==1][col]
    sns.kdeplot(no_resp, ax=axes[i], label='Not Interested (0)', color=BLUE, fill=True, alpha=0.35, linewidth=2)
    sns.kdeplot(resp,    ax=axes[i], label='Interested (1)', color=PINK, fill=True, alpha=0.45, linewidth=2)
    axes[i].axvline(no_resp.mean(), color=BLUE, linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5, label=f'Mean 0: {no_resp.mean():.1f}')
    axes[i].axvline(resp.mean(),    color=PINK, linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5, label=f'Mean 1: {resp.mean():.1f}')
    mean_diff_pct = abs(resp.mean() - no_resp.mean()) / (no_resp.mean() + 1e-9) * 100
    axes[i].set_title(f'{col}\nMean diff: {mean_diff_pct:.1f}%', fontweight='bold')
    axes[i].legend(fontsize=8)

plt.suptitle('Step 10 — Bivariate Analysis: Continuous Features vs Response\n'
             'Age shows a real mean shift → moderate predictor. Vintage nearly overlaps → weak standalone predictor.',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

📌 Observation: age shows the clearest separation — interested customers average ≈43.4 years vs ≈38.2 for uninterested (a ~14% mean difference). annual_premium distributions almost fully overlap. vintage is essentially identical between the two classes, confirming Step 8's near-zero-skew, uniform-looking distribution carries little signal.

💡 Engineering insight: age is worth binning into life-stage buckets (e.g. young/mid/senior) to let tree models split on the non-linear age–response relationship more cleanly than a single numeric threshold would.

Step 11 — Outlier Detection by Response Status¶

Why: Outliers affect model training differently by class. If concentrated in one class, removing them is harmful — those are genuine customers, not data errors. We clip rather than remove.

Business insight: A ₹500K+ annual premium is a real high-net-worth customer, not a data-entry error. Dropping these rows would silently remove the company's most valuable accounts from the training set.

In [11]:
cont_cols = ['age', 'annual_premium', 'vintage']
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 6))
outlier_summary = []

for i, col in enumerate(cont_cols):
    q1 = df[col].quantile(0.25); q3 = df[col].quantile(0.75); iqr = q3 - q1
    lower = q1 - 1.5*iqr; upper = q3 + 1.5*iqr
    n_out   = ((df[col] < lower) | (df[col] > upper)).sum()
    pct_out = n_out / len(df) * 100
    out_in_1 = ((df[df['response']==1][col] < lower) | (df[df['response']==1][col] > upper)).sum()
    outlier_summary.append({'feature': col, 'total_outliers': n_out,
                            'pct_of_data': round(pct_out, 2), 'outliers_in_response=1': out_in_1})
    df.boxplot(column=col, by='response', ax=axes[i],
               boxprops=dict(color=BLUE), medianprops=dict(color=PINK, linewidth=2.5),
               whiskerprops=dict(color=BLUE), capprops=dict(color=BLUE),
               flierprops=dict(marker='o', markerfacecolor=GRAY, markersize=3, alpha=0.5))
    axes[i].set_title(f'{col}\n{n_out} outliers ({pct_out:.1f}%)', fontweight='bold')
    axes[i].set_xlabel('response (0=No, 1=Yes)')

plt.suptitle('Step 11 — Outlier Detection by Response Status (IQR Method)\n'
             'Clipping preserves all rows while controlling scale distortion. Never remove outliers here.',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print('Outlier Summary:'); display(pd.DataFrame(outlier_summary))

Outlier Summary:
feature total_outliers pct_of_data outliers_in_response=1
0 age 0 0.00 0
1 annual_premium 10320 2.71 1555
2 vintage 0 0.00 0

📌 Observation: The outlier summary table shows annual_premium has all 10,320 IQR outliers in the dataset (2.71% of rows) — age and vintage contribute zero. Of those 10,320 annual_premium outliers, 1,555 belong to customers who responded "Yes" (response=1) — roughly 15% of the outlier rows convert, above the 12.26% base rate, confirming these are genuine high-value customers rather than data errors worth discarding.

💡 Pipeline decision: IQR Clipper on annual_premium at fold=1.5, fitted on training data and applied to test using training statistics only — prevents leakage. age and vintage skip the clipping step entirely since they have no outliers to control.

Step 12 — Skewness Analysis and Power Transformation¶

Why: Linear models assume approximately normal feature distributions. PowerTransformer reduces skewness and improves model coefficient stability.

Business insight: Applying the transform only inside the scaled preprocessor is a key architectural decision — tree models (RF, XGBoost, LightGBM) are skew-invariant and would gain nothing from it.

In [12]:
from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer
skew_cols = ['annual_premium']
pt = PowerTransformer(method='yeo-johnson')
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 8))

for i, col in enumerate(skew_cols):
    raw = df[col].dropna().values.reshape(-1, 1)
    transformed = pt.fit_transform(raw).flatten()
    sk_before = df[col].skew(); sk_after = pd.Series(transformed).skew()
    improvement = abs(sk_before) - abs(sk_after)
    sns.histplot(df[col], kde=True, bins=40, ax=axes[0], color=PINK, edgecolor='white')
    axes[0].set_title(f'{col} — BEFORE\nskewness = {sk_before:.3f}', fontweight='bold')
    sns.histplot(transformed, kde=True, bins=40, ax=axes[1], color=GREEN, edgecolor='white')
    axes[1].set_title(f'{col} — AFTER PowerTransform\nskewness = {sk_after:.3f} (↓{improvement:.2f})', fontweight='bold')

plt.suptitle('Step 12 — Skewness Reduction via Yeo-Johnson PowerTransformer\n'
             'Applied ONLY to scaled preprocessor (linear/distance models). Tree models use raw clipped values.',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

📌 Observation: PowerTransformer reduces annual_premium skewness from ≈1.77 to close to 0 — making it suitable for Logistic Regression, SVM, and KNN.

💡 Pipeline decision: Dual preprocessor — scaled branch (Clipper + PowerTransformer + StandardScaler) for linear/distance models vs unscaled branch (Clipper only) for tree models. Both fitted on training data only.

Step 13 — Statistical Significance Testing (Mann-Whitney U + Cohen's d)¶

Why: Visual differences may not be statistically significant. Mann-Whitney U is non-parametric (no normality assumption, appropriate given the skew found in Step 8). Cohen's d measures practical significance — a statistically significant but tiny effect may not matter for a ranking model.

Business insight: With 381K rows, even trivial differences become "statistically significant" — effect size (Cohen's d) is what actually tells telecalling ops whether a feature is worth acting on.

In [13]:
test_cols = ['age', 'annual_premium', 'vintage']
results = []
for col in test_cols:
    g0 = df[df['response']==0][col].dropna()
    g1 = df[df['response']==1][col].dropna()
    _, p = mannwhitneyu(g0, g1, alternative='two-sided')
    d = (g1.mean() - g0.mean()) / (np.sqrt((g0.std()**2 + g1.std()**2) / 2) + 1e-9)
    results.append({'feature': col, 'mean_no': round(g0.mean(),2), 'mean_yes': round(g1.mean(),2),
                    'p_value': round(p,6), 'significant': '✅ YES' if p<0.05 else '❌ NO',
                    'cohens_d': round(abs(d),3),
                    'effect_size': 'Large' if abs(d)>0.8 else 'Medium' if abs(d)>0.5 else 'Small'})

sig_df = pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values('cohens_d', ascending=False)
print('Statistical Significance + Effect Size:'); display(sig_df)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
colors = [PINK if p < 0.05 else GRAY for p in sig_df['p_value']]
bars   = ax.barh(sig_df['feature'], sig_df['cohens_d'], color=colors, edgecolor='white')
ax.axvline(0.2, color=GRAY, linestyle=':', linewidth=1.5, label='Small (d=0.2)')
ax.axvline(0.5, color=BLUE, linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5, label='Medium (d=0.5)')
ax.axvline(0.8, color=PINK, linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5, label='Large (d=0.8)')
for bar, d in zip(bars, sig_df['cohens_d']):
    ax.text(d + 0.005, bar.get_y() + bar.get_height()/2, f'd={d:.3f}', va='center', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_title("Step 13 — Effect Size (Cohen's d) per Feature\n"
             'Pink = statistically significant (p<0.05). Even the strongest continuous feature is only a small effect.',
             fontweight='bold')
ax.set_xlabel("Cohen's d"); ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Statistical Significance + Effect Size:
feature mean_no mean_yes p_value significant cohens_d effect_size
0 age 38.18 43.44 0.000000 ✅ YES 0.373 Small
1 annual_premium 30419.16 31604.09 0.000000 ✅ YES 0.066 Small
2 vintage 154.38 154.11 0.516301 ❌ NO 0.003 Small

📌 Observation: The significance table shows all three continuous features are statistically significant (p<0.001 for age and annual_premium; vintage is the one exception at p=0.516, confirming it carries no signal). But Cohen's d stays small throughout: age d=0.373 (mean 43.44 for responders vs 38.18 for non-responders — the largest effect in this table), annual_premium d=0.066 (mean 31,604 vs 30,419), vintage d=0.003 (essentially no difference, 154.11 vs 154.38). This confirms the real signal in this dataset lives in the categorical/binary features (Step 9), not the continuous ones.

💡 Business insight: A model relying only on age/premium/vintage would perform poorly — previously_insured and vehicle_damage must carry most of the predictive weight, matching the SHAP feature-importance ranking expected from the trained model.

Step 14 — Feature Correlation with Target (Point-Biserial)¶

Why: Point-biserial correlation measures linear association between a feature and the binary target. Direction matters for business interpretation — negative means higher value → less likely to respond.

In [14]:
num_cols = ['age', 'driving_license', 'previously_insured', 'annual_premium',
            'policy_sales_channel', 'vintage']
corr_results = []
for col in num_cols:
    r, p = pointbiserialr(df['response'], df[col].fillna(df[col].median()))
    corr_results.append({'feature': col, 'correlation': round(r,4), 'p_value': round(p,6),
                         'direction': 'Positive ↑' if r > 0 else 'Negative ↓'})

corr_df = pd.DataFrame(corr_results).sort_values('correlation', key=abs, ascending=False)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 5))
colors = [PINK if r > 0 else BLUE for r in corr_df['correlation']]
bars   = ax.barh(corr_df['feature'], corr_df['correlation'], color=colors, edgecolor='white')
ax.axvline(0, color='black', linewidth=1)
for bar, r in zip(bars, corr_df['correlation']):
    offset = 0.008 if r > 0 else -0.008; ha = 'left' if r > 0 else 'right'
    ax.text(r + offset, bar.get_y() + bar.get_height()/2, f'{r:.4f}', va='center', fontsize=9, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_title('Step 14 — Feature Correlation with Target (Point-Biserial r)\n'
             'previously_insured is the single strongest predictor in the dataset, and it is negative.',
             fontweight='bold')
ax.set_xlabel('Point-Biserial Correlation with response')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print('\nAll correlations:'); display(corr_df)

All correlations:
feature correlation p_value direction
2 previously_insured -0.3412 0.000000 Negative ↓
4 policy_sales_channel -0.1390 0.000000 Negative ↓
0 age 0.1111 0.000000 Positive ↑
3 annual_premium 0.0226 0.000000 Positive ↑
1 driving_license 0.0102 0.000000 Positive ↑

📌 Observation: previously_insured (r≈-0.34) is the strongest predictor by a wide margin, followed by policy_sales_channel (r≈-0.14) and age (r≈0.11). vintage is essentially uncorrelated (r≈-0.001), confirming Step 10 and Step 13.

💡 Pipeline decision: SelectKBest with mutual_info_classif is preferred over a plain correlation cutoff — it will also pick up vehicle_damage's strong non-linear/interaction signal, which point-biserial correlation on its own encoding may understate.

Step 15 — Feature Correlation Matrix¶

Why: Inter-feature correlations reveal multicollinearity. Highly correlated features carry redundant information — hurts linear model interpretability without improving prediction.

Business insight: previously_insured and vehicle_damage are expected to correlate with each other (a currently-insured vehicle is less likely to have unresolved damage) — worth confirming before treating them as two fully independent signals.

In [15]:
df_corr = df.copy()
df_corr['gender_enc']         = df_corr['gender'].map({'Male': 1, 'Female': 0})
df_corr['vehicle_damage_enc'] = df_corr['vehicle_damage'].map({'Yes': 1, 'No': 0})
df_corr['vehicle_age_enc']    = df_corr['vehicle_age'].map({'< 1 Year': 0, '1-2 Year': 1, '> 2 Years': 2})

corr_cols = ['age', 'driving_license', 'previously_insured', 'annual_premium',
             'policy_sales_channel', 'vintage', 'gender_enc', 'vehicle_damage_enc',
             'vehicle_age_enc', 'response']
corr_matrix = df_corr[corr_cols].corr()
mask        = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr_matrix, dtype=bool))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 9))
sns.heatmap(corr_matrix, mask=mask, annot=True, fmt='.2f',
            cmap='RdBu_r', center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1,
            linewidths=0.5, linecolor='white', annot_kws={'size': 9}, ax=ax, square=True)
ax.set_title('Step 15 — Feature Correlation Matrix (Lower Triangle)\n'
             'Red=positive, Blue=negative. |r|>0.5 = multicollinearity concern for linear models.',
             fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

high_corr = []
for i in range(len(corr_matrix.columns)):
    for j in range(i):
        r = corr_matrix.iloc[i, j]
        if abs(r) > 0.4:
            high_corr.append({'feature_1': corr_matrix.index[i], 'feature_2': corr_matrix.columns[j], 'r': round(r,4)})
if high_corr:
    print('\nFeature pairs with |r| > 0.4:')
    display(pd.DataFrame(high_corr).sort_values('r', key=abs, ascending=False))
else:
    print('\nNo feature pairs exceed |r| > 0.4 among features (excluding target).')

Feature pairs with |r| > 0.4:
feature_1 feature_2 r
1 vehicle_damage_enc previously_insured -0.8241
2 vehicle_age_enc age 0.7658
0 policy_sales_channel age -0.5778
3 vehicle_age_enc policy_sales_channel -0.5507

📌 Observation: The high-correlation table reveals stronger multicollinearity than a quick glance at the heatmap suggests: vehicle_damage_enc ↔ previously_insured r=-0.824 (customers who are already insured almost never report vehicle damage), vehicle_age_enc ↔ age r=0.766 (older customers own older vehicles), policy_sales_channel ↔ age r=-0.578, and vehicle_age_enc ↔ policy_sales_channel r=-0.551. vehicle_damage_enc also shows the strongest correlation with response of any encoded feature in this matrix — but it is not independent of previously_insured.

💡 Pipeline decision: No feature is dropped for redundancy at this stage — the |r|=0.82 pair is flagged for the Step 20 VIF check rather than removed outright, since VIF (which accounts for the full feature set jointly, not just one pair) is the more reliable test for whether this correlation is actually destabilizing a linear model. SelectKBest(k=8) also provides a second line of defense against any remaining redundancy during model training.

Step 16 — High-Cardinality Features: Region Code & Policy Sales Channel¶

Why: region_code (53 levels) and policy_sales_channel (155 levels) cannot be one-hot encoded without exploding the feature space — but they are not noise either. Aggregating response rate per code reveals whether certain regions or channels systematically over/under-perform.

Business insight: If a handful of channels concentrate almost all the volume and the response rate, telecalling operations can prioritize agent capacity toward those channels immediately, independent of any model.

In [16]:

                    color=[PINK if v > overall else BLUE for v in channel_rate.values], edgecolor='white')

             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')

Top-10 channels cover 91.9% of all customers
Top-10 regions   cover 63.9% of all customers

📌 Observation: The top-10 channels cover 91.9% of all customers, while the top-10 regions cover only 63.9% — channel is far more concentrated. Within that concentration, response rate varies enormously by channel: channel 152 (134,784 customers, the single largest channel) converts at only 2.86%, while channel 26 (79,700 customers) converts at 19.94% and channel 163 (a much smaller channel, 2,893 customers) converts at 30.42% — a >10× spread across channels of very different sizes. Region codes vary far less: the top-10 regions range from 6.27% to 18.72%, clustering closer to the 12.26% overall rate, with region 28 (106,415 customers, by far the largest region) standing out at 18.72%.

💡 Pipeline decision: policy_sales_channel → target-mean encoding (fit on training folds only, to avoid leakage) since it carries real, wide-ranging signal even among high-volume channels. region_code → frequency encoding — its variation is milder, and frequency alone captures most of what a target encoding would add, with region 28's outsized volume and above-average rate as the main exception worth monitoring.

Step 17 — Interaction Effect: Previously Insured × Vehicle Damage¶

Why: Individual feature analysis (Step 9) shows both previously_insured and vehicle_damage are powerful alone. The real question for a scoring model is whether their combination is even more extreme — a 2×2 heatmap makes any such interaction immediately visible.

Business insight: If one combination of these two flags converts at near-zero and another converts many times the baseline, this pair alone is enough to build a zero-cost pre-filter rule that a model only refines at the margins.

In [17]:

Response rate table (%):

previously_insured

📌 Observation: The full 2×2 response-rate table reads: previously_insured=0, vehicle_damage=No → 3.79%, previously_insured=0, vehicle_damage=Yes → 25.01%, previously_insured=1, vehicle_damage=No → 0.04% (effectively never converts), previously_insured=1, vehicle_damage=Yes → 0.87%. previously_insured dominates the outcome — even with damage history, an already-insured customer converts at under 1% — while vehicle_damage is what separates the two previously_insured=0 sub-segments by roughly 6.6×.

💡 Pipeline decision: Engineer an explicit previously_insured_x_damage interaction feature (4-category concatenation) so that tree-based models don't have to rediscover this 2-way split from scratch across many splits — and expose the previously_insured=1 & vehicle_damage=No combination to business ops as a standalone "do not call" pre-qualification rule.

Step 19 — Engineered Features Preview¶

Why: Validating that engineered features provide better class separation than raw features before adding pipeline complexity. If the engineered feature shows a clearer response-rate spread than either input alone, it earns its place in the pipeline.

Business insight: previously_insured_x_damage operationalizes the Step 17 finding directly into a single categorical feature the model can split on in one step, instead of needing two sequential splits.

💡 Pipeline decision: Keep previously_insured_x_damage and age_group as engineered features feeding the model; drop premium_per_vintage_day from the shortlist — the added complexity isn't earning its keep next to the stronger interaction term.

Step 20 — Multicollinearity Check (VIF)¶

Why: VIF quantifies variance inflation from feature correlation. VIF > 10 means a feature is nearly a linear combination of others — it provides no independent information to a linear model.

Business insight: A clean VIF profile means Logistic Regression coefficients (used for a simple, auditable baseline scorecard alongside the tree model) will be stable and interpretable for the underwriting team.

In [20]:
vif_cols = ['age', 'driving_license', 'previously_insured', 'annual_premium',
            'policy_sales_channel', 'vintage', 'gender_enc', 'vehicle_damage_enc', 'vehicle_age_enc']
X_vif = df_corr[vif_cols].fillna(df_corr[vif_cols].median())
X_vif = add_constant(X_vif)
vif_data = pd.DataFrame({
    'feature': X_vif.columns,
    'VIF': [variance_inflation_factor(X_vif.values, i) for i in range(X_vif.shape[1])]
}).iloc[1:].sort_values('VIF', ascending=False)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
colors = [PINK if v>10 else '#FF9800' if v>5 else GREEN for v in vif_data['VIF']]
bars = ax.barh(vif_data['feature'], vif_data['VIF'], color=colors, edgecolor='white')
ax.axvline(5,  color='#FF9800', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5, label='VIF=5 (moderate)')
ax.axvline(10, color=PINK,      linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5, label='VIF=10 (severe)')
for bar, v in zip(bars, vif_data['VIF']):
    ax.text(v + 0.1, bar.get_y() + bar.get_height()/2, f'{v:.1f}', va='center', fontsize=9, fontweight='bold')
ax.set_title('Step 20 — Variance Inflation Factor (Multicollinearity)\n'
             'Green=safe(<5) · Orange=moderate(5-10) · Pink=severe(>10)',
             fontweight='bold')

The Step 15 pairwise correlations (up to |r|=0.82) do raise the VIF of the two features involved, but not past the moderate band — the correlation is not compounding across the wider feature set.

💡 Pipeline decision: No features are excluded on VIF grounds — even the highest-VIF pair (vehicle_damage_enc, previously_insured) stays well below the severe threshold, so Logistic Regression coefficients remain stable. SelectKBest(mutual_info_classif, k=8) is still applied for dimensionality control once region_code/policy_sales_channel encodings and engineered features are added to the matrix.

Step 21 — SMOTENC Class Balancing Preview¶

Why: Visualizing before/after SMOTENC confirms the resampling strategy achieves the intended balance. Three panels show train-before, train-after, and test-untouched — demonstrating correct methodology.

Business insight: The test set must retain the real 12.3% response rate. Evaluating on an artificially balanced test set would overstate recall and give false confidence that the model catches more real leads than it actually would in production.

In [21]:
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTENC
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

model_df = df_corr.copy()
model_df['vehicle_age_enc'] = model_df['vehicle_age_enc'].astype(int)
feature_cols = ['age', 'driving_license', 'previously_insured', 'annual_premium',
                'policy_sales_channel', 'vintage', 'gender_enc', 'vehicle_damage_enc', 'vehicle_age_enc']
X = model_df[feature_cols]
y = model_df['response']

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42)
cat_indices = [X.columns.get_loc(c) for c in
               ['driving_license', 'previously_insured', 'gender_enc', 'vehicle_damage_enc', 'vehicle_age_enc']]
smote = SMOTENC(categorical_features=cat_indices, random_state=42)
X_res, y_res = smote.fit_resample(X_train, y_train)

def bar_plot(ax, counts, title):
    bars = ax.bar(['Not Interested (0)', 'Interested (1)'], counts.values, color=[BLUE, PINK], edgecolor='white', width=0.5)
    for bar, v in zip(bars, counts.values):
        ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width()/2, bar.get_height() + max(counts.values)*0.01, f'{v:,}',
                ha='center', fontweight='bold', fontsize=11)
    ax.set_title(title, fontweight='bold'); ax.set_ylabel('Count'); ax.set_ylim(0, max(counts.values) * 1.2)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 5))
bar_plot(axes[0], y_train.value_counts().sort_index(),
         f'Train BEFORE SMOTENC\nImbalance: {y_train.value_counts()[0]/y_train.value_counts()[1]:.1f}:1')
bar_plot(axes[1], pd.Series(y_res).value_counts().sort_index(), 'Train AFTER SMOTENC\nBalanced 1:1')
bar_plot(axes[2], y_test.value_counts().sort_index(), 'Test set — UNTOUCHED\nReal imbalance for honest evaluation')
plt.suptitle('Step 21 — SMOTENC Class Balancing (Train Only)\n'
             'SMOTENC respects mixed feature types. Test set never resampled — reflects real-world distribution.',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f'Train before : {dict(y_train.value_counts().sort_index())}')
print(f'Train after  : {dict(pd.Series(y_res).value_counts().sort_index())}')
print(f'Test set     : {dict(y_test.value_counts().sort_index())}  ← imbalanced, as expected')

Train before : {0: 267519, 1: 37368}
Train after  : {0: 267519, 1: 267519}
Test set     : {0: 66880, 1: 9342}  ← imbalanced, as expected

📌 Observation: SMOTENC achieves 50:50 balance in training while respecting the binary nature of driving_license, previously_insured, gender_enc, vehicle_damage_enc, and the ordinal vehicle_age_enc. The test set retains its true 7.2:1 imbalance — intentional and correct for honest evaluation.

💡 Why SMOTENC over SMOTE: The feature set mixes binary/ordinal flags with continuous fields (age, annual_premium). Plain SMOTE would interpolate impossible values like previously_insured=0.6. SMOTENC handles categorical/ordinal columns via majority voting in synthetic samples, keeping every generated row valid.
